questions.q: The editorial recalls Swami Vivekananda’s reply to a lady in Chicago who judged him by his clothes. What was his point?
options: Monks should not be judged at all
Not quite. The article says: It is character, not tailoring, that makes a gentleman.
Americans care too little about religion
Not quite. The article says: It is character, not tailoring, that makes a gentleman.
Indian clothes are finer than Western ones
Not quite. The article says: It is character, not tailoring, that makes a gentleman.
It is character, not tailoring, that makes a gentleman
Yes. “A gentleman is, as a gentleman does.”
questions.rationale: He said: “In your country the tailor makes a man a gentleman; but in my country, character makes a man a gentleman.”

questions.q: Why, according to the editorial, do crimes flourish in a rights-conscious society and stay in check in a duty-conscious one?
options: Rights-conscious societies are poorer
Not quite. The article says: A rights-conscious person knows only his own needs; a duty-conscious person thinks of the needs of society.
A rights-conscious society has too few laws
Not quite. The article says: A rights-conscious person knows only his own needs; a duty-conscious person thinks of the needs of society.
Duty-conscious people fear punishment more
Not quite. The article says: A rights-conscious person knows only his own needs; a duty-conscious person thinks of the needs of society.
A rights-conscious person knows only his own needs; a duty-conscious person thinks of the needs of society
Exactly. Laws alone – “paper activism” – cannot do this.
questions.rationale: “A rights-conscious person only knows his/her own needs, whereas a duty-conscious person thinks about the needs of society.”

questions.q: Light, gravity and magnetism cannot be seen directly; they are known by their effects. What does the article conclude from this about religious truths?
options: Only what a microscope or telescope shows is real
Not quite. The article says: Inference is as sound as direct observation, so reasoning from design to a Designer is scientific.
Science has nothing to say about unseen things
Not quite. The article says: Inference is as sound as direct observation, so reasoning from design to a Designer is scientific.
Religious truths need no reasoning at all
Not quite. The article says: Inference is as sound as direct observation, so reasoning from design to a Designer is scientific.
Inference is as sound as direct observation, so reasoning from design to a Designer is scientific
Well reasoned. The same method is used in science itself.
questions.rationale: “Man was compelled to accept that indirect, or inferential argument, was academically and intellectually as sound as direct argument. This change… has, in the present age, made divine reasoning truly scientific.”

questions.q: What, according to the article, happens when a person observes silence?
options: He loses touch with reality
Not quite. The article says: He stops conversing with the outer world and begins conversing with his inner world.
His mind becomes empty and at rest
Not quite. The article says: He stops conversing with the outer world and begins conversing with his inner world.
He stops conversing with the outer world and begins conversing with his inner world
Right. Man is never silent “for himself.”
He gives others room to speak
Not quite. The article says: He stops conversing with the outer world and begins conversing with his inner world.
questions.rationale: “Remaining silent as far the external world goes, he starts conversing with his internal world… He eschews superficiality and engages himself with deeper realities.”

questions.q: How does the article argue from man’s experience of himself to belief in God?
options: Man is part of God and shares His powers
Not quite. The article says: Man knows will, sight, hearing and an “I” in himself, so he can conceive a Being who has these to a perfect degree.
Man cannot know himself, so he cannot deny God
Not quite. The article says: Man knows will, sight, hearing and an “I” in himself, so he can conceive a Being who has these to a perfect degree.
Man knows will, sight, hearing and an “I” in himself, so he can conceive a Being who has these to a perfect degree
Yes. Believing in God is likened to believing in one’s own self.
Man is weak, so he needs to imagine a protector
Not quite. The article says: Man knows will, sight, hearing and an “I” in himself, so he can conceive a Being who has these to a perfect degree.
questions.rationale: “Man’s experience of himself, his attributes, his characteristics, make it possible for him to apprehend the eternal Being who possesses these very attributes… to a superlative degree.”

questions.q: The article speaks of a farmer who wants to reap on the very day he sows. What does this picture warn against?
options: Saving too much for the future
Not quite. The article says: Seeking in this world the rewards that belong to the next, and so losing both.
Trusting the weather instead of God
Not quite. The article says: Seeking in this world the rewards that belong to the next, and so losing both.
Working without rest
Not quite. The article says: Seeking in this world the rewards that belong to the next, and so losing both.
Seeking in this world the rewards that belong to the next, and so losing both
Correct. Today is for action; tomorrow is for the harvest.
questions.rationale: “The world of today is a place for action, and the world of tomorrow is the place for reaping the harvest… Man desires to achieve in the present world, what is to be achieved in tomorrow’s world. This is the reason he loses both.”

questions.q: After studying more than a hundred disasters, which word did the Disaster Research Centre find best described how people behave?
options: Resignation
Not quite. The article says: Heroism.
Panic
Not quite. The article says: Heroism.
Heroism
Yes – “heroism, not panic or shock.”
Shock
Not quite. The article says: Heroism.
questions.rationale: The report said human beings are “amazingly controlled and resilient in the face of adversity. Perhaps heroism, not panic or shock, is the right word.” The article asks us not to waste time lamenting losses.

questions.q: Before the battle of Uhud the Prophet preferred to stay and defend Madinah, while most companions wished to go out. What did he do, and what does the article take from it?
options: He kept to his own view, showing a leader must decide alone
Not quite. The article says: He went with the majority – showing consultation and majority opinion at work in Islam.
He let each companion act as he wished
Not quite. The article says: He went with the majority – showing consultation and majority opinion at work in Islam.
He went with the majority – showing consultation and majority opinion at work in Islam
Well done. The Quran says believers’ affairs are decided by mutual consultation (42:38).
He delayed the decision until revelation came
Not quite. The article says: He went with the majority – showing consultation and majority opinion at work in Islam.
questions.rationale: “Sometimes the Prophet accepted the opinion of the majority, even though it was against his personal opinion. One such example is found at the time of the battle of Uhud.”

questions.q: Steel can be trusted to hold up a bridge because its properties never change. What parallel does the article draw for human society?
options: Modern society depends mainly on engineering
Not quite. The article says: Society is stable only when people show a consistent, reliable character.
Society needs strong rulers as a bridge needs steel
Not quite. The article says: Society is stable only when people show a consistent, reliable character.
Society is stable only when people show a consistent, reliable character
Exactly. A man’s worth lies in keeping his character under all conditions.
People, like materials, cannot change their nature
Not quite. The article says: Society is stable only when people show a consistent, reliable character.
questions.rationale: “If people do not show consistency, reliability and predictability in their character, human society will crumble.”

questions.q: Thelma Thompson came to love the Mojave desert she had wanted to leave. What had changed?
options: Her husband was posted elsewhere
Not quite. The article says: Only her own attitude – she chose to see “the stars” rather than “the mud”.
The climate became milder
Not quite. The article says: Only her own attitude – she chose to see “the stars” rather than “the mud”.
The local people learned English
Not quite. The article says: Only her own attitude – she chose to see “the stars” rather than “the mud”.
Only her own attitude – she chose to see “the stars” rather than “the mud”
Yes. Nothing outside her had changed.
questions.rationale: “Neither the desert, nor the natives, nor any other element in the situation had changed. Whatever change had taken place was inside the mind and heart of Thelma Thompson.”
